aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.
dyk: ...that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) had to register as a foreign agent over a roughly $5,000 contract to write four op-eds about the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce — while [AIPAC](/wiki/aipac), he notes, does not have to register at all?

...that [Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) says members of Congress fear [AIPAC](/wiki/aipac) because the threat is not defeat but erasure — *"you will never work in politics ever again"* — and names [Thomas Massie](/wiki/thomas-massie) as one of the few who took it?
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.body:
[John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) identifies the exemption of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee from the Foreign Agents Registration Act as the structural fact underlying its influence: [AIPAC](/wiki/aipac) *"is the only group of its kind that does not have to register as a foreign agent."*<Cite t="1:22:52" />

## The op-eds

His contrast is drawn from his own record. Around 2008 Kiriakou took a small contract — he puts it at five or six thousand dollars — to write four op-eds in support of the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce: pieces arguing that Abu Dhabi was business-friendly, welcoming to Americans, and a place where everyone made money. Because he was publishing in support of a foreign entity, he was required to register as a foreign agent.<Cite t="1:22:52" /><Cite t="1:23:23" />

His question follows directly from the comparison: *"what the heck is AIPAC doing 24/7?"*<Cite t="1:23:23" />

## The mechanism of fear

Kiriakou describes elected officials as *"very afraid"* of the organisation, and locates the fear specifically in the threat of being primaried. Pressed on why a member would not simply absorb one primary loss, his answer is that the threat is larger than a single race: *"they're saying you will never work in politics ever again — we will hound you for the rest of your career."*<Cite t="1:23:23" /><Cite t="1:23:54" /><Cite t="1:24:24" />

Asked who among them has the courage to go first, he names [Thomas Massie](/wiki/thomas-massie), whom he saw about a week before that primary. He counts Marjorie Taylor Greene as a partial case who did not see it through, saying she quit halfway.<Cite t="1:23:54" />

9-11-plea-agreements.title: 9/11 plea agreements
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.
dyk: ...that per [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou), the 9/11 defendants could never be tried on the merits because [torture](/wiki/enhanced-interrogation) made every confession inadmissible — *"there's no evidence against them. None."*?

...that the [9/11 plea agreements](/wiki/9-11-plea-agreements) included a promise not to move [Khalid Sheikh Mohammed](/wiki/khalid-sheikh-mohammed) and his co-defendants to the Colorado supermax, because they said they could not cope with the cold and preferred to stay in [Guantanamo](/wiki/guantanamo-bay)?
9-11-plea-agreements.body:
The **9/11 plea agreements** were deals reached during the Biden administration with the most senior [Guantanamo](/wiki/guantanamo-bay) detainees accused of plotting the September 11 attacks — [Khalid Sheikh Mohammed](/wiki/khalid-sheikh-mohammed) among them — and subsequently vacated. [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) treats them as the predictable end point of the [torture programme](/wiki/enhanced-interrogation).<Cite t="1:11:23" /><Cite t="1:12:26" />

## Terms

The defendants agreed to plead guilty to terrorism — to the murder of 2,976 people — in exchange for life without parole. The second element of the bargain, as Kiriakou describes it, was a promise not to transfer them to the supermax facility in Colorado: they said they could not deal with the cold and wanted to remain in Cuba, because it is warm.<Cite t="1:11:23" /><Cite t="1:11:55" /><Cite t="1:12:26" />

The Secretary of Defense vacated the agreements on the grounds that the authority to make such a deal was his alone. The matter went through the courts, which threw the deals out. Kiriakou's observation is that the outcome is unchanged in substance — the men have life without parole either way, and are never going to be released.<Cite t="1:11:55" /><Cite t="1:12:58" />

## Why a plea at all

Kiriakou's explanation for why the government negotiated rather than tried the case is that there was nothing left to try it with. The defendants confessed, but confessed under torture, which makes every statement inadmissible: *"there's no evidence against them. None."* His allocation of blame is unambiguous — *"you have to blame the CIA for that. If the CIA hadn't tortured these guys…"*<Cite t="1:10:51" /><Cite t="1:13:29" /><Cite t="1:13:59" />

He extends the point into a general objection to indefinite detention without charge: if the detainees are as dangerous as the government says, then charge them, try them, and sentence them. *"We won't even charge people in our country who are committing a crime."*<Cite t="1:10:20" />

## The families

Kiriakou is sympathetic to the 9/11 families' opposition to any deal — *"I understand, I get it, I really do"* — while treating the outcome they want as unavailable: *"it's never going to happen. We're a country of laws. We can't just pretend that we're a country of laws except when the laws aren't convenient for us."*<Cite t="1:12:58" /><Cite t="1:13:29" />
